strengths: The paper provides a theoretically grounded contribution: Proposition 1 (multi-modal ELBO surgery) and Corollary 2 give a precise decomposition of when the proposed bound is an approximate lower bound on the joint log-likelihood, and Remark 5 contrasts this with the known irreducible variational gap of mixture-based bounds (Daunhawer et al., 2022), which strengthens the motivation.

The permutation-invariant aggregation schemes (DeepSets/SumPooling, Set Transformer, and permutation-equivariant variants for private latents) are a natural and well-motivated generalization of PoE/MoE, grounded in the exchangeability characterization of Bloem-Reddy and Teh (2020); they allow handling arbitrary modality subsets without exponential cost in the number of modalities, unlike MoPoE.

The work is unusually comprehensive: an information-theoretic rate-distortion perspective (Lemma 7, Corollary 8), optimal variational distributions (Remark 10), mixture-prior extensions with an optimal categorical variational factor, missing-modality handling, a weak identifiability result (Proposition 15) connecting multi-modal conditioning to iVAE-style identifiability, and connections to neural processes in Appendix B.

Experiments are broad and careful: linear-Gaussian models with analytically computable LLH against true MLE, nonlinear identifiable synthetic models with MCC, missing-modality settings, and MNIST-SVHN-Text with controlled hyperparameters across all bound/aggregation combinations plus external baselines (MVAE, MMVAE, MoPoE, MMJSD, MVTCAE), including rate-distortion trade-off analysis.

The limitations section is honest: it acknowledges the extra cost of sampling from two encoding distributions, higher computational cost of learned aggregation, and that mixture-based bounds may be preferable when cross-modal reconstruction is the primary goal.
weaknesses: The headline claim of a 'tighter variational bound' must be qualified: Corollary 2 shows the bound is only approximate, with a residual term that is not necessarily negative, and tightness requires the encoder consistency condition KL(q_agg(z_\S|x_\S)||q(z|x_\S)) = 0. The central advantage is thus conditional on properties that cannot be verified in practice, and empirical LLH gains should be interpreted with this caveat (the paper is transparent about this, but it weakens the strength of the claim).

Novelty is partly incremental: the combined marginal+conditional objective is a generalization of Wu and Goodman (2019) to arbitrary numbers of modalities and masks, permutation-invariant aggregation via DeepSets/Set Transformers is standard tooling applied to a new setting, and the conditional-prior/learned-prior ideas closely mirror neural processes and VampPrior work. The identifiability result is explicitly a translation of Lu et al. (2022) to the multi-modal setting.

The most realistic experiment (MNIST-SVHN-Text) yields only modest improvements: coherence gains are described as 'slightly more coherent for SVHN to Text, but less coherent for MNIST', and the large discrepancy between reported LLH values and prior baselines is attributed to decoder variance choices, which limits comparability with the literature. MMVAE+ (Palumbo et al., 2023) is compared only theoretically (Remark 25), not empirically, despite being the closest competing bound.

Presentation is dense and at times inconsistent: e.g., the main text references 'Corollary 19' before it is defined (it appears as Corollary 2 in the main body and Corollary 19 in the appendix), there are typographical issues ('multi-model', Figure 1 caption 'indeterminancy'), and Proposition 1 is stated as a wall of coupled equations that is hard to parse without the appendix.

Reproducibility is only partial: implementation details, architectures, and hyperparameters are commendably thorough (Appendices J-N), and prior code is reused, but no explicit code release or repository link is stated, which is important given the many interacting design choices (masking distribution rho, STL gradient estimators, stop-gradient usage).

strengths: The paper provides a careful and largely honest theoretical treatment: Proposition 1 gives a multi-modal extension of ELBO surgery with marginal and conditional distribution-matching decompositions, and Remarks 3-6 transparently discuss when the proposed objective is (and is not) a valid lower bound, including the prior-hole / aggregated-posterior mismatch that the conditional term can induce.

The theoretical comparison with mixture-based bounds is a genuine contribution: the authors build on Daunhawer et al. (2022) to show that their conditional objective can become tight in the infinite-capacity limit for an arbitrary number of modalities, whereas the variational gap of mixture bounds grows with modality diversity.

The rate-distortion interpretation (Lemma 7, Corollary 8) for the marginal and conditional (cross-) rates and distortions is a nice complementary lens and is supported empirically via the full/cross reconstruction and rate plots in Figure 3.

Experiments are comparatively thorough and well-controlled for the main claims: linear-Gaussian settings with an analytic ground-truth MLE LLH, MCC-based identifiability evaluation for nonlinear identifiable models (shared and private latents, missing modality rates), and MNIST-SVHN-Text with matched hyperparameters across bounds and aggregation schemes, including parameter-matched PoE+/MoE+ baselines.

Limitations are discussed candidly (higher gradient cost, added compute of learnable aggregation, mixed coherence results), and architectural/hyperparameter details are reported at a level that aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central headline claim of 'tighter variational bounds' is overstated: the proposed objective L_S + L_\S is only an approximate lower bound on the log-likelihood. The cross-entropy term in Corollary 2 is not necessarily negative, and the bound is tight only under consistency conditions (e.g., q_φ(z|x_S) = aggregated posterior) that are not enforced during optimization. The paper is honest about this, but the abstract and introduction present it more strongly than the theory supports.

There is internal tension between the theory and the empirical narrative: Remark 4 argues that maximizing L_\S induces exactly the encoder/aggregated-posterior mismatch that harms cross-generation, yet Section 5 reports improved cross-generation for the proposed bound. The conditions under which the mismatch is benign in practice are not analyzed, leaving the mechanism behind the empirical gains unexplained.

Originality is modest. The conditional bound is a straightforward generalization of the MVAE objective of Wu and Goodman (2019) to arbitrary masks, and the permutation-invariant aggregators are direct applications of DeepSets (Zaheer et al., 2017) and Set Transformers (Lee et al., 2019). The identifiability result (Proposition 15) is explicitly an adaptation of Theorem 4 of Lu et al. (2022) to the multi-modal setting. The contribution is a competent combination of known components rather than a new method or fundamentally new understanding.

Editing and presentation quality is below bar for the main track: dangling or garbled sentences (e.g., 'and for any and that H_S ≤ R_S + D_S' on p.9), inconsistent cross-references to the same corollary as 'Corollary 2' in the main text but 'Corollary 19' in Remarks 3 and 5 and Appendix A, and dense, notation-heavy exposition in Sections 2-4 that makes the key assumptions hard to track.

The real-data evaluation is limited to a single benchmark (MNIST-SVHN-Text), where the results are mixed: the proposed bound improves joint LLH and SVHN cross-generation but yields slightly lower MNIST coherence, and external baselines are only loosely comparable because of differing decoder variances and hyperparameters, which the authors themselves acknowledge. No code release is stated, which limits reproducibility given the number of implementation-specific choices (reweighting of likelihoods, Laplace likelihoods, mixture handling).

The connection to the identifiability contribution (Section 4.1) is thin: Proposition 15 applies to conditional posteriors under restrictive exponential-family assumptions, and the paper offers only informal arguments (points (a), (b) before Section 4.2) that the proposed inference actually improves identifiability, with empirical support limited to MCC on synthetic data.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely useful and well-grounded contribution: a new multi-modal variational objective (Eq. 3-4, the 'masked' bound L_S + L_{\S}) that generalizes the MVAE-style joint bound of Wu & Goodman (2019) to arbitrary numbers of modalities, and shows formally (Corollary 19, Remark 5) that it can be tight for infinite-capacity encoders whereas mixture-based bounds have an irreducible gap (Daunhawer et al., 2022).

The distribution-matching analysis (Proposition 1, 'multi-modal ELBO surgery') is a nice theoretical contribution that extends the classic Hoffman & Johnson decomposition to the conditional/multi-modal case, clarifying when the encoders are Bayes-consistent and linking the mismatch to the prior-hole / cross-generation problem (Remarks 3-4).

The information-theoretic treatment (Lemma 7, Corollary 8, Remarks 9-10) gives a clean rate-distortion interpretation, including the conditional/cross rate R_{\S}, and characterizes the optimal variational densities for both the proposed and mixture-based objectives.

The permutation-invariant aggregation schemes (SumPooling/DeepSets, Set Transformer) are well-motivated via the exchangeability characterization of Bloem-Reddy & Teh (2020), and the permutation-equivariant extension for private latent variables (Section 3.2, Examples 3-5) is a thoughtful design that keeps private latents insensitive to unobserved modalities.

The weak identifiability result (Proposition 15, translated from Lu et al. 2022) is carefully stated with explicit assumptions and honest remarks (Remarks 16-18) about what is and is not identified, including the non-injectivity issue for private latents.

Experiments are thorough and well-controlled: linear Gaussian models with analytically computable MLE log-likelihoods validate the claim that the new bound attains higher true LLH than mixture bounds for fixed aggregation; nonlinear identifiable simulations show improved MCC; and the MNIST-SVHN-Text study carefully fixes hyperparameters across methods to disentangle the effect of the objective from that of the aggregation, with matched-parameter baselines (PoE+/MoE+).

The limitations are discussed candidly (higher gradient cost from two encoding samples, more expensive learned aggregation, and that mixture bounds may be preferable when cross-modal reconstruction is the priority), which increases trust in the reported trade-offs.

Reproducibility support is strong: full architectures (Tables 15-20), training details, pseudo-code for gradient estimators (Algorithms 1-2), and references to the JAX/Flax implementations and data generation procedures.
weaknesses: The proposed objective is only an approximate lower bound on the joint log-likelihood: the residual term in Corollary 19 is not necessarily negative, and tightness requires either exact posteriors or KL(q*_phi_{\S}(z|x_S)||q_phi(z|x_S)) = 0, which is not enforced during training. The paper is honest about this, but in practice the claimed 'tighter variational bound' benefit rests on this approximation, and no diagnostic is provided to measure how close to a true bound the learned models are.

Empirical gains on the real dataset (MNIST-SVHN-Text) are mixed rather than decisive: the proposed bound improves SVHN/Text cross-generation and joint LLH, but mixture bounds yield better cross-reconstructions and often better MNIST-side coherence, and SelfAttention does not uniformly improve LLH (Table 5). The practical advantage therefore depends on the target metric, which somewhat dilutes the headline claim.

The comparison to external baselines (MVAE, MMVAE, MoPoE, MMJSD) is only via previously reported numbers under different decoder variance assumptions, which the authors themselves acknowledge limits interpretability (Table 7 discussion); a re-trained baseline under matched variances would have strengthened the evidence.

The bound requires sampling from two encoding distributions per gradient step, so the method is strictly more expensive than mixture-based bounds; no wall-clock or cost-controlled comparison is reported, so it is unclear how much of the LLH gain comes simply from added computation.

Presentation is dense: the notation (double-indexed bounds, aggregated posteriors q^agg, q*, masks) is heavy and some results (e.g., Corollary 2 vs Corollary 19 duplication, Remarks 20-22) could be streamlined; readers will need the appendices to follow the main claims.

Novelty is incremental in parts: the conditional bound structure follows Wu & Goodman (2019) and the PI constructions are direct applications of DeepSets/Set Transformer theory; the strongest originality lies in the ELBO-surgery analysis and the identifiability connection rather than in the architectures themselves.

The stated focus on MCAR missingness (Section 4.3) leaves the practically important non-random missingness case unaddressed, and the multi-task-learning gradient balancing ideas mentioned in Remark 6 are not explored empirically.
